topicName: Relational Algebra and Logical Query Processing
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Relational Algebra and Logical Query Processing"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding relational algebra is foundational for advanced SQL tuning. While SQL is a declarative language (you specify what data you want), the database engine translates your query into procedural operations using relational algebra. Mastering this translation allows you to write queries that the query optimizer can parse and execute efficiently."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Relational Algebra Operators in SQL"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Relational algebra consists of several primary operators that map directly to standard SQL constructs:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Selection (Sigma): Corresponds to the SQL WHERE clause. It filters rows based on a predicate."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Projection (Pi): Corresponds to the SQL SELECT clause. It filters columns, reducing the width of the dataset."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Join (bowtie): Corresponds to INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, etc. It combines relations based on a common attribute."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Union, Intersection, and Difference: Map directly to UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT set operators."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Logical Query Processing Phases"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"When the database engine processes a query, it follows a strict logical sequence that differs significantly from the written syntax order. The logical processing order typically flows as follows:"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"1. FROM clause (including JOINs and Cartesian products)"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"2. ON filter clauses"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"3. OUTTER rows (if outer joins are used)"},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"4. WHERE clause"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"5. GROUP BY clause"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"6. HAVING clause"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"7. SELECT clause (including window functions and aliases)"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"8. DISTINCT clause"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"9. ORDER BY clause"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"10. LIMIT / OFFSET clause"},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical SQL Tuning Implications"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because of logical processing order, column aliases defined in the SELECT phase cannot be referenced in the WHERE phase. Understanding this prevents common errors and helps in optimizing performance. For example, filtering early (Pushdown Predicate) reduces the intermediate dataset size before expensive joins or aggregations take place."},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) as avg_sal
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date > '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the code snippet above, the WHERE clause filters rows before aggregation (GROUP BY), which is far more efficient than attempting to filter aggregated metrics that belong in the HAVING clause. Always apply selective predicates as early in the logical pipeline as possible."}]
